modules.title: Mastering Your Civil Servant Salary
modules.summary: Understand every line of your payslip: basic pay, allowances, NAPSA, PAYE, and the "take-home" trap that catches most civil servants.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Zambian civil servant payslip
lessons.content:
# Anatomy of a Zambian civil servant payslip

Most civil servants read only the number at the bottom of the payslip. That is the one number you cannot change. The lines above it tell you what you are really being paid, what is being taken, and - most usefully - what you can plan with.

## The lines that matter

| Line | What it is | The rule that applies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basic pay | The fixed salary for your grade and notch | The base for NHIMA |
| Allowances | Housing, transport, utility, commuted car, education, rural hardship, shift/on-call | **Taxable** - they are added to your emoluments for PAYE |
| Gross pay | Basic pay + all allowances + any one-off payments | The base for PAYE and for NAPSA |
| PAYE | Income tax withheld and paid to ZRA on your behalf | Progressive bands on the **full gross** |
| NAPSA (employee 5%) | Pension contribution | 5% of gross monthly earnings, capped at K1,861.80 a month in 2026 |
| NHIMA (employee 1%) | Compulsory health cover | 1% of **basic salary** only - no ceiling |
| Other deductions | Union dues, salary-deducted loans, salary advances | Read every one of them |
| Net pay | What reaches your account | **Budget on this number and no other** |

## NAPSA: 5% of gross, and the 2026 ceiling

NAPSA takes 5% of your **gross monthly earnings** - a wider base than basic pay. It includes basic pay, bonuses, commissions, severance pay, overtime, leave pay and acting allowances. Your employer adds a matching 5%, so 10% of your pay goes into your pension each month, and the employer's half does not reduce your take-home pay.

| NAPSA, 2026 charge year | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Monthly insurable earnings ceiling | K37,236.00 |
| Maximum employee contribution (5%) | K1,861.80 |
| Matching employer contribution (5%) | K1,861.80 |
| Combined maximum | K3,723.60 |

The 2025 figures were a K34,164 ceiling, K1,708.20 each and K3,416.40 combined. Some websites still repeat the old K28,920.30 ceiling, so treat any number that is not the 2026 one as out of date.

## NHIMA: 1% of basic, with no ceiling

NHIMA is 1% of **basic salary**, not gross. Your allowances sit outside the base, and NHIMA has **no earnings ceiling**. Your employer adds a matching 1%.

Two rules that save arguments at the clinic: there is a **4-month waiting period** after registration before a fully paid member can access NHIMA services (no waiting period at 65 and above), and a dependant who turns 18 must register as a principal and contribute separately.

## The 1 January 2025 change most people have not noticed

Since **1 January 2025**, under the *Income Tax (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 2024*, the employee relief for pension contributions was removed. **NAPSA and NHIMA no longer reduce the amount your PAYE bands are applied to.** PAYE is charged on your **full gross**, and NAPSA and NHIMA are deducted alongside it, not before it.

Several Zambian payroll consultancies still deduct NAPSA before computing PAYE, which understates your PAYE. If your payslip shows PAYE reduced by your NAPSA deduction, query it with your payroll office and with ZRA.

## A worked example: K15,000 gross, K15,000 basic

| Step | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Gross salary | K15,000.00 |
| PAYE (worked out in the next lesson) | -K3,176.00 |
| NAPSA employee, 5% of gross | -K750.00 |
| NHIMA employee, 1% of basic | -K150.00 |
| **Net take-home** | **K10,924.00** |

You keep about 73% of gross. Your employer adds roughly K900 more on top of that - K750 of employer NAPSA money and K150 of employer NHIMA money - so the true cost of employing you is about 6% above your gross.

## Three habits

1. **Keep every payslip.** Twelve a year is the evidence you need when you query a deduction.
2. **Check two numbers every month:** that gross equals basic plus allowances, and that PAYE was computed on the full gross.
3. **Budget on net pay.** Gross is what the employer spends on you. Net is what you can spend.

PAYE, NAPSA and NHIMA deductions are all due to the relevant authority by the **10th of the month following** the month they relate to.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write down the four numbers on your payslip - basic, gross, PAYE, net - and keep them in one place.
> 2. Check whether your PAYE was computed on your full gross; if it was reduced by your NAPSA deduction, ask your payroll office to check it against ZRA.
> 3. Optional: ask NAPSA for your contribution statement and confirm you have no missing months on record.

> **Where to check**
> The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) for PAYE, the National Pension Scheme Authority (NAPSA) for the K37,236 ceiling, and NHIMA for the 1% basic-salary base and the 4-month waiting period.

lessons.title: PAYE tax bands explained (with examples)
lessons.content:
# PAYE tax bands explained (with examples)

PAYE ("Pay As You Earn") is the income tax your employer withholds from your pay and hands to the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) for you. The single most important thing to understand is that the bands are **progressive**: each slice of your income is taxed at its own rate. You do not pay 37% on your whole salary just because you earn more than K9,200.

## The 2026 charge-year bands

| Monthly taxable emoluments (K) | Rate | Annual equivalent (K) | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 - 5,100 | 0% | up to 61,200 | 0% |
| 5,100.01 - 7,100 | 20% | 61,201 - 85,200 | 20% |
| 7,100.01 - 9,200 | 30% | 85,201 - 110,400 | 30% |
| Above 9,200 | 37% | Above 110,400 | 37% |

The **tax-free threshold is K5,100 a month** (K61,200 a year). The bands did not change in the 2026 budget, which took effect on 1 January 2026. The monthly tax credit for differently abled persons is **K600 a month**.

## Worked examples

**K6,500 a month.** The first K5,100 is tax-free. The remaining K1,400 is taxed at 20%, so PAYE = **K280**.

**K9,000 a month.** K5,100 at 0% = K0. The next K2,000 at 20% = K400. The next K1,900 at 30% = K570. PAYE = **K970**, an effective rate of 10.8%.

**K10,000 a month.** K0 + K400 (20% on K2,000) + K630 (30% on K2,100) + K296 (37% on the K800 above K9,200). PAYE = **K1,326**, an effective rate of 13.3%.

**K15,000 a month.** K0 + K400 + K630 + K2,146 (37% on the K5,800 above K9,200). PAYE = **K3,176**, an effective rate of 21.2%.

Notice how far the effective rate sits below the top band rate, and how slowly it climbs.

## The marginal-rate trap

"If I earn K10,000, why is my PAYE not 37% x K10,000 = K3,700?" Because only the **K800 above K9,200** is taxed at 37%. Everything below that keeps its own lower rate. That is what "marginal" means.

A raise makes the same point. Moving from K9,200 to K9,700, the extra K500 is taxed at 37% = K185. You keep K315 of the K500. Plan for the net figure, not the gross one.

## The rule that changed on 1 January 2025

Since the *Income Tax (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 2024* came into operation, the employee relief for pension contributions was removed. **PAYE is charged on your full gross.** NAPSA and NHIMA are deducted **alongside** your PAYE, not before it. Some payroll consultancies still deduct NAPSA first and therefore understate PAYE - if yours does, ask your payroll office and ZRA to check.

And remember that allowances are taxable. If your employer pays your rent, electricity or school fees directly, that amount is added to your emoluments and taxed.

## Six other PAYE facts worth knowing

| Situation | How it is treated |
| --- | --- |
| A second or subsequent job | Treated as part-time: taxed at the top rate of **37%**, with no tax credits |
| A bonus | Taxed in the month you receive it - it can push part of it into the 37% band |
| Back pay (arrears) | Normally taxed in the months it was earned, not as one lump |
| Over-withholding in a year | PAYE is refundable - ask your employer or ZRA; employers keep payroll records for **6 years** after the charge year |
| The NHIMA 1% | Charged on basic salary, not gross, and it does **not** reduce your PAYE base |
| The tax credit | K600 a month for differently abled persons |

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Recompute your PAYE by hand from your gross using the four bands above, then compare it with the figure on your payslip.
> 2. If the two do not match, write the difference down and raise it with your payroll office before the next payday.
> 3. Optional: write the four band thresholds and the K600 credit on the wall you look at every month.

> **Where to check**
> The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA), through your employer or the ZRA TaxOnline portal, for the charge-year bands and for any PAYE query.

lessons.title: The salary trap and how to escape it
lessons.content:
# The salary trap and how to escape it

The salary trap is not poverty. It is a cycle, and it catches civil servants on perfectly good salaries:

1. **Payday.** The money lands. You feel rich.
2. **Days 6 to 20.** Bills, school fees, transport, relatives. You feel fine.
3. **Days 21 to 28.** You are short. You take a small mobile money loan, or an advance from a colleague.
4. **Next payday.** The deduction comes out before you spend anything, and the cycle restarts.

After a year of that cycle you have paid a lot of interest and saved nothing.

## Why it happens

- **Lifestyle inflation.** Every raise is matched by extra spending, so you are never actually richer.
- **Social pressure.** The moment you get a raise, half your compound knows.
- **No buffer.** Every surprise - a car repair, a hospital bill, a funeral - has to be financed, because only about one adult in nine in Zambia says savings is their main source of emergency money, while more than one in three says family or friends.
- **Credit is instant.** A mobile money loan takes seconds and nobody has to approve you, which is exactly why the price is so high.

## What the trap really costs

Borrowing is not free, and the arithmetic is worth doing once. A K100,000 bank personal loan over 12 months at 30% per annum means you receive K100,000 and repay **K130,000** - K10,833 a month instead of the K8,333 it would be if the money were free. That is **K2,500 a month, K30,000 in total**, for the use of K100,000 for one year.

The informal version is worse. A "10% a month" flat charge on a K5,000 loan over four weeks means you repay K5,500 - and if that rate compounded monthly for a year it would be **214% a year**.

This is why the Bank of Zambia has warned about public workers in public. It found "an alarming rise in non-performing loans linked to public workers", with off-payroll borrowing, non-disclosure of existing obligations and multiple borrowing across institutions. The Bank has told lenders to apply debt-service-ratio limits strictly, and told payroll administrators to strengthen payroll controls.

## Four habits that break the cycle

**1. Pay yourself first, on payday.** Your PAYE, NAPSA and NHIMA are already deducted at source, so your net pay lands in one place on one day. Move your saving out on that same day, before you spend anything. A standing order does this without relying on willpower.

**2. Save by division, not by will.** For a goal with a date - school fees, a funeral, a laptop - divide the cost by the number of paydays left and transfer that amount every payday. K18,000 over 9 paydays is K2,000 a month, automatically, including the months when something has gone wrong. If it does not divide evenly, round up.

**3. Use a separate wallet, not a separate tab.** 65.8% of Zambian adults save using mobile money and only 15.4% at a bank. Money in the wallet you shop from is money you spend. A second wallet, ideally on a different phone number so it is not on your main screen, is invisible at the point of spending.

**4. Do not borrow to build savings.** Start with a small fixed amount instead. K100 on the 28th of every month, every month, for six months, is K600 - and it is a habit.

## Two figures to keep in your head

- **Inflation is 6.1% (September 2026).** The Bank of Zambia reports that the real savings rate only turned positive in February 2026, so a savings account paying 2-4% is losing buying power, not making it.
- **The Bank of Zambia's policy rate is 10.75%** (from 30 September 2026). The 6-month deposit rate is **7.4%** and the average commercial bank lending rate is **27.5%** (June 2026). Save first, borrow second.

## One last trap: the cost of sending money home

From 1 January 2026 the mobile money levy roughly doubled on most bands - from **K0.32** on the first K150 up to **K10.00** on transfers above K10,000. It applies to **person-to-person transfers only**, the **sender** pays it, and it sits **on top of** the operator's own fee. It is not a tax on your salary and it is not charged when you pay a merchant. If your relatives expect money every month, agree the real, all-in cost before you promise them a figure.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Work out your true monthly payment - goal divided by paydays left - and set that transfer for payday in a separate account or wallet.
> 2. List every loan and advance you owe (lender, balance, rate, next due date) on one page, and set a standing order of K100 to a second wallet you do not shop from.
> 3. Optional: ask whoever you send money to each month what the all-in mobile money cost is, and adjust the amount you promise.

> **Where to check**
> The Bank of Zambia (policy rate page, and the quarterly *Interest Rates and Bank Charges* booklet) for inflation, deposit and lending rates, and your mobile money operator's published tariff for fees.

modules.title: The Debt Trap: Mobile Money Loans, Sakawa & Pyramid Schemes
modules.summary: The single biggest financial threat to Zambian civil servants is not low income - it is predatory debt. Learn to spot the traps, and how to get out of one.

lessons.title: Why civil servants are the #1 target for predatory lenders
lessons.content:
# Why civil servants are the #1 target for predatory lenders

Predatory lenders do not target you because you are careless. They target you because a civil servant's salary is the most reliable, most visible and most easily collected income in Zambia - and in 2026 the Bank of Zambia said so publicly.

## What the Bank of Zambia found

Its financial stability assessments found "an alarming rise in non-performing loans linked to public workers". Some public workers were taking **off-payroll credit** - borrowing that never touches your salary record - "beyond permissible limits, often through misrepresentation, non-disclosure of existing obligations, and multiple borrowing across institutions".

The response matters to you directly:

- Lenders must "strictly adhere to debt-service-ratio limits and adopt responsible lending practices", and credit bureau data must be used consistently. Compliance with debt-service-ratio limits and affordability standards "is mandatory".
- Payroll administrators are told to strengthen internal payroll controls and to take disciplinary action where abuse of payroll-based deduction arrangements is found.

The Bank also found some lenders had "inconsistent use of the Credit Reference Bureau (CRB), or disregard of data from the Bureau altogether". Your file exists, and lenders are now directed to read it.

## Why the salary is attractive to a lender

Your pay is fixed and dated, your employer can collect repayments at source, and your employment record can be confirmed. On top of that, Zambia has one licensed credit reference agency, CRB Africa, licensed by the Bank of Zambia under the *Credit Reporting Act No. 8 of 2018*.

That cuts both ways. A lender who checks your file sees your other loans. A lender who does not check is offering you money they do not expect you to repay, and charging you for it.

## What credit actually costs in Zambia

| Source | Rate | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial banks, average lending rate | **27.5%** (June 2026) | Range across the market 3.7% - 31.0% |
| Salary-backed personal loans | **11.00% - 37.00%** | Bank of Zambia published averages as at 31 March 2026 |
| Savings groups / chilimba | 5% - 20% **per month** | Published benchmarks |
| Microfinance institutions | 4% - 10% **per month** | Some also quote 25% - 50% per annum |
| Money-lender (Money-Lenders Act, Cap 398) | Capped at **48% per year** | Above that is presumed harsh and unconscionable, and **compound interest is illegal** |

The 11.00% is Bank of China Zambia and the 37.00% is First Alliance Bank. These are published averages, not offers - always ask for a written quote.

## Do the arithmetic yourself

**Bank loan.** K100,000 over 12 months at 30% per annum: you receive K100,000 and repay **K130,000**. That is K10,833 a month against the K8,333 it would be if the money were free - **K2,500 a month, K30,000 in total**.

**Informal lender.** A "10% a month" flat charge on K5,000 over four weeks: you repay K5,500. If that rate compounded monthly for a year it would be **214% a year**.

**The law.** Under the Money-Lenders Act (Cap 398) a lender must give you a **written contract before the money is lent**, and you can demand a **loan statement** at any time. Interest above 48% a year is unlawful. A lender who refuses both has already answered your question.

## The five warning signs

1. You are borrowing from a new lender because a payment is due on an old one.
2. You are using one credit card or mobile money overdraft to pay another.
3. You do not know the total balance of your borrowing, only that you are behind.
4. You are paying a fee to *access* a loan, before any money is released.
5. The lender does not check the credit bureau, or asks you not to disclose other loans.

## Three rules

- **Your salary is your strongest financial asset. Do not attach it to more than one expensive loan.**
- **Never borrow from a lender who does not check the credit bureau.** If they do not check, they do not know what you owe, and they will lend to you again.
- **Compare on total repayable, not on the monthly instalment.** A small instalment on a long term is how people end up paying double.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write down every loan you owe - lender, balance, rate, monthly payment, next due date - on one page, and total the monthly repayments.
> 2. Ask each lender for the total amount you will repay and for a written contract, then compare that figure with the monthly instalment you were offered.
> 3. Optional: ask a bank or SACCO for a written quote against your own savings and see how it compares with your cheapest and most expensive borrowing.

> **Where to check**
> The Bank of Zambia (its public notice on public-worker loan delinquency, and the quarterly *Interest Rates and Bank Charges* booklet) and the Credit Reference Bureau Africa record that the Bank of Zambia licenses for credit reference services.

lessons.title: Sakawa, MMM-style pyramids, and the "K100 → K50,000" lie
lessons.content:
# Sakawa, MMM-style pyramids, and the "K100 → K50,000" lie

Start with the words: they are what you need when you report.

## What "sakawa" actually means

In Zambia, **sakawa** is the popular word for a **Ponzi or pyramid scheme** - an "empowerment" offer where early investors are paid out of the money later investors bring in. It is not another word for a fee you pay upfront.

The official Zambian legal term is a **"money circulation scheme"**. Section 157 of the Banking and Financial Services Act says that a person shall not "conduct, or participate in, a money circulation scheme; or issue a notice, circular, prospectus, proposal or other document inviting the public to subscribe to a money circulation scheme". **Conducting or participating in one is an offence.**

The Securities and Exchange Commission of Zambia (under the *Securities Act No. 41 of 2016*) uses "Ponzi scheme" and "pyramid scheme", and gives one rule of thumb: **"The moment they ask you to recruit others, just know there is a problem."**

Advance-fee fraud is a **different crime** - a promise of a contract, loan, prize or fund that needs a small fee first. Report it to the police or CCPC as advance-fee fraud, not as sakawa.

## The Bank of Zambia's definition, in plain English

> "A money circulation scheme is an unsustainable investment operation that pays returns to its investors from their own money or the money paid by subsequent investors, rather than from profit earned by the individual or organization running the operation."

That is the whole scam: no business, no product - only money moving from the newest joiner to the oldest, and an ever-increasing flow of new money needed to keep it going.

## Why the "K100 to K50,000" promise cannot work

Put in K100, get K50,000 out. If ten people join and each is paid K50,000, that is K500,000 needed - and ten people paying in K100 each is K1,000. The gap is filled only by finding more people, and everyone who joins after the queue stops moving loses everything they paid in. Your money is the return, which is why the scheme always ends in a queue.

## The five-question test

1. **Where does the return come from?** "From new investors" means a money circulation scheme. A real return comes from real economic activity.
2. **Is the return "guaranteed" or "fixed"?** Real returns vary. A guaranteed 50% a month is not an investment.
3. **Is the operator licensed?** Check SEC's "Find a Licensee" register, and the Bank of Zambia's licensed institutions for anything taking deposits.
4. **Can you withdraw your principal at any time?** If not, your money is locked in with the operator.
5. **Are you being asked to recruit others?** That is SEC's own published test. The answer is always no.

Any one "no" above: walk away. Be fair though: a genuine chilimba of 4 to 20 members, with fixed contributions and a set rotation order, is not a pyramid - but a chilimba "does not serve as a safety net in emergencies". Keep emergency money in your own account.

## If you are already in one

1. **Stop sending money.** Even if they promise that one more payment "unlocks" the next level. That is the trap, not the exit.
2. **Screenshot everything** - the chats, the payment confirmations, the transaction IDs and the numbers.
3. **Report it in the right words:** "money circulation scheme" or "Ponzi scheme" to SEC and the Bank of Zambia; "advance-fee fraud" for a fee-first promise.

| Channel | Route |
| --- | --- |
| ZICTA - report a scammer's number or a stolen phone | \*707# |
| ZICTA - check how many SIMs are on your NRC | \*101# |
| ZICTA call centre | 7070 |
| CCPC consumer complaints | 5678 |
| Police | nearest station / cyber-crimes unit |
| SEC Zambia | seczambia.org.zm and the "Find a Licensee" register |
| Bank of Zambia | boz.zm, +260 211 399 300, info@boz.zm |

Report fast, with evidence: screenshots, the transaction ID and the receiving number.

## Why this matters to you in particular

Between 2023 and the first half of 2024 the Zambia Police Service recorded **1,124 online scam cases** worth over **K38,948,000** - about **K34,700 lost per case**, one to two months of a civil servant's net salary.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Save three numbers on your phone: \*707# to report a scammer, \*101# to check your SIM registrations, and 5678 for consumer complaints.
> 2. Before sending money to any "investment group", run the five-question test and check SEC's "Find a Licensee" register.
> 3. Optional: ask one member of your savings group to show you their written rules, including whether the organiser takes a cut.

> **Where to check**
> The Securities and Exchange Commission of Zambia (licence register and public alerts), the Bank of Zambia (public warnings on money circulation schemes), and the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission on 5678.

lessons.title: How to escape a debt spiral (the 90-day reset)
lessons.content:
# How to escape a debt spiral (the 90-day reset)

If you are already in a spiral - several loans, salary-deducted repayments, advances from colleagues - there is a route out. It is uncomfortable and it takes one quarter. This is the plan.

## Day 1: the honest list

One page. For each debt write down: the lender, the balance owed, the rate, the monthly payment, the next due date, and what happens if you miss a payment.

Add the monthly payments together. That total has to fit inside your net pay. If it does not, you are over-committed, not merely behind, and no amount of effort fixes it while the total stays there.

## Day 2: stop new borrowing

No exceptions, for 90 days. No small mobile money loan. No "just this once" advance. No "I will pay it back next month".

**Do not borrow to build savings either.** Funding an emergency fund with borrowed money is how a K10,000 problem becomes a K50,000 problem.

## Days 3 to 7: sort the debts into two piles

**Pile 1 - lawful, documented debt.** A bank loan, a SACCO loan, a cooperative loan. You have a written contract, a known rate and a real business on the other end.

**Pile 2 - unlawful or predatory debt.** Interest above 48% a year, compound interest, no written contract, a fee demanded before the money is released, threats, or a lender who refuses a loan statement. Under the Money-Lenders Act (Cap 398) a lender must give you a **written contract before the money is lent**, and you can demand a **loan statement** at any time. Interest above 48% a year is presumed harsh and unconscionable.

Handle pile 2 first, and do not pay a penny more into it without a written settlement.

## Days 8 to 14: negotiate, and use the law

**With a bank.** Ask for hardship restructuring in writing - a smaller monthly amount for a set period, then back to normal. A bank would rather restructure a loan than write it off and recover nothing.

**Remember who regulates the lenders.** Zambia has one licensed credit reference agency, Credit Reference Bureau Africa, licensed by the Bank of Zambia under the *Credit Reporting Act No. 8 of 2018*. Under the Bank of Zambia's 2020 credit information Directive, lenders must submit your information to the Bureau and must use Bureau data when assessing credit above **K500**. If a lender did not check, they did not know what you owe.

**If a negative listing is wrong, you can challenge it.** Write to the agency, which must send the credit provider an endorsed copy of your report within 5 days and investigate within 14 days; the Bank of Zambia can then intervene. Information is normally kept for 10 years from final repayment.

**Complain about a bank to the Bank of Zambia.** A written complaint to the Manager-Banking is acknowledged within 2 working days and resolved within 10 working days.

**If a court order or salary attachment exists, do not ignore it.** Get legal advice and ask for a payment plan through your lawyer. Regular small payments are far better for you than a default.

## Days 15 to 30: rebuild the buffer

Set up a separate wallet for emergency money and put a small fixed amount in it every payday. This is the step that stops you re-entering the spiral. A savings circle is good for a goal with a date, but it is not an emergency fund - keep that in your own account.

## Days 30 to 60: pay down in the right order

**Highest interest rate first.** Each debt you clear releases its minimum payment, and you roll that into the next one. Where two debts are close in rate, clear the smaller balance first for the psychological win.

Do not pay a debt with your pension. Taking 20% or 30% of your NAPSA contributions early permanently reduces the pension you will receive and lowers the minimum-pension floor you can fall back on. Work out the monthly pension first, then the lump sum. And check that you have 180 monthly contributions on record - missing months can cost you the right to a pension at all.

## Days 60 to 90: roll over

By now one or two debts should be gone. Review the total remaining, the interest paid this quarter and the next three months of repayments. Then set the new rule: one salary-backed loan at a time, and nothing off-payroll. That is the rule the Bank of Zambia is really asking public workers to keep.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Complete the one-page debt list above and total your monthly repayments, then compare that total with your net pay.
> 2. Write to your highest-rate lender asking for the total repayable figure and a written contract, and write to your bank asking for a hardship option in writing.
> 3. Optional: check your credit file with Credit Reference Bureau Africa and challenge anything that is wrong.

> **Where to check**
> The Bank of Zambia (its public notice on public-worker loan delinquency, its supervision of credit reporting, and its Customer Service Charter complaints route) and your own lenders for the written contract, loan statement and hardship terms.
